MARC PAUL NOORDMAN, MARIUS VAN DER PUT, AND JAAP TOP
Abstract. The problem of algebraic dependence of solutions to (non-
linear) ﬁrst order autonomous equations over an algebraically closed ﬁeld
of characteristic zero is given a ‘complete’ answer, obtained indepen-
dently of model theoretic results on diﬀerentially closed ﬁelds. Instead,
the geometry of curves and generalized Jacobians provides the key ingre-
dient. Classiﬁcation and formal solutions of autonomous equations are
treated. The results are applied to answer a question on Dn-ﬁniteness
of solutions of ﬁrst order diﬀerential equations.
1. Introduction and summary
Let C be an algebraically closed ﬁeld of characteristic zero. For a linear
diﬀerential equation of order n over (say) the diﬀerential ﬁeld (C(z), d
dz),
there is an extension of diﬀerential ﬁelds PV F ⊃C(z), called a Picard–
Vessiot ﬁeld, such that C is also the ﬁeld of constants of PV F and PV F is
‘minimal’ such that the equation has linearly independent solutions y1, . . . , yn
over C. For any extension of diﬀerential ﬁelds PV F ⊆L, the y1, . . . , yn
form a basis, now over the ﬁeld of constants of L, of all solutions in L of the
equation. The transcendence degree of PV F over C(z) is at most n2.
The algebraic relations between these solutions and their derivatives are
measured by the diﬀerential Galois group. This linear algebraic group sub-
group of GLn(C) will, in general, become smaller if C(z) is replaced by a
diﬀerential ﬁeld extension. For details, see for example [18].
For non-linear diﬀerential equations, the theory of Galois groupoids, de-
veloped by B. Malgrange, H. Umemura and many others, replaces the usual
diﬀerential Galois groups (see for instance [4] and references therein). It is
concerned with solutions and their algebraic relations. Here we will study
the simplest type of non-linear equations: autonomous ﬁrst order diﬀerential
equations
P(u, u′) = 0
where P ∈C[X, Y ] is irreducible, involves both X and Y and u′ stands for
du
dz . The theory of Galois groupoids does not seem to shed much light on
these equations. The following example of M. Rosenlicht [15] shows that
non-linear diﬀerential equations are rather diﬀerent from linear ones.

of distinct non-constant solutions of (X, ω) in a diﬀerential ﬁeld F ⊃C is

Proposition 3.3. Any diﬀerential equation (X, ω) of general type is, in a
unique way, the pull back of a new diﬀerential equation of general type.
Proof. By deﬁnition, the classes of exact, exponential type and Weierstrass
type 1-forms are closed under pull-back. Hence, if ω is the pull-back of some
eω, then eω must be of general type as well. Hence, it suﬃces to show that ω
is the pull-back of some new 1-form.

(X′, ω′) we have to show that an inﬁnite chain of pull backs is not possible.

ω = ϕ∗ω′. Then ω′ has at least 1 zero, since it is of general type. A local

ﬁeld U with ﬁeld of constants C. Indeed one can take for U the diﬀerential
closure of the ﬁeld K(y).
In this way, we can produce many additional
solutions for this diﬀerential equation, without increasing the subﬁeld of
constants. We expect the same phenomenon to occur for all autonomous
equations of general type.
This is in contrast with the situation for systems of linear equations and
for equations of exact, exponential and Weierstrass type: for those types of
equations, adding new solutions to K introduces new constants.
7. Dn-finiteness of solutions
Let K be a diﬀerential ﬁeld (of characteristic 0) with algebraically closed
ﬁeld of constants C.
An extension of diﬀerential ﬁelds F ⊃K is called
an iterated Picard–Vessiot extension if there exists a sequence of diﬀerential
ﬁelds F = Kn ⊃· · · ⊃K1 ⊃K0 = K where each extension Ki+1 ⊃Ki is a
Picard–Vessiot extension.
From the literature, especially [10], we adopt the following deﬁnitions:
An element ξ ∈C((z)) is D-ﬁnite (over C(z)) if it satisﬁes a linear scalar
diﬀerential equation with coeﬃcients in C(z).
For n > 1 we inductively
deﬁne ξ to be Dn-ﬁnite (over C(z)) if ξ satisﬁes a linear scalar diﬀerential
equation with coeﬃcients which are Dn−1-ﬁnite. An element ξ ∈C((z)) is
called D-algebraic (over C(z)) if there is a non-trivial polynomial relation
P(ξ(m), ξ(m−1), . . . , ξ, z) = 0 with coeﬃcients in C between the derivatives
of ξ and z.
One easily veriﬁes that a Dn-ﬁnite element ξ lies in the iterated Picard–
Vessiot extension of C(z) deﬁned by all the linear scalar equations involved
in the Dn-property of ξ.
In [10] it is shown that Dn-ﬁniteness deﬁnes strictly increasing subsets of
C((z)). A natural question is:
Is there a D-algebraic element which is not Dn-ﬁnite for any n ≥1?
The positive answer is given in Proposition 7.1.
Proposition 7.1. Let ξ ∈C((z)) be a non-constant solution of an au-

any iterated Picard-Vessiot extension of C(z). In particular, ξ is not Dn-

Abstract: The problem of algebraic dependence of solutions to (non- linear) ﬁrst order autonomous equations over an algebraically closed ﬁeld of characteristic zero is given a ‘complete’ answer, obtained indepen- dently of model theoretic results on diﬀerentially closed ﬁelds. The results are applied to answer a question on Dn-ﬁniteness of solutions of ﬁrst order diﬀerential equations.
